Modeling and analysis of nonlinear dynamic buckling-type vibrations in an auxetic rotating polygonal metamaterial
abstract: Auxetic rotating polygons are instrumental for programmable design of metamaterials with tunable proprieties. Their particular configuration leads to a sudden but controlled transformation between different states. However, opposed to the conventional perspective of the static stability in the pre-buckling state, a dynamic buckling-type phenomenon is observed in experiments based on a finite rotating-polygonal network. Under harmonic excitations much lower than the static buckling limit, global longitudinal motions and local rotations contribute to the buckling-type deformation of the system. In this paper, we report this phenomenon and we develop an analytical discrete nonlinear model to understand this phenomenon. The discrete model parameters are rigorously identified and validated against finite element simulations, achieving good agreement in both static force–displacement responses and linearized modal analyses. Based on the analytical discrete model, the phenomenon is reproduced in dynamic simulations with nonlinear jump resonances on both ends of the rotation-excited branch where the global longitudinal mode is coupled with the local rotational mode. Our work not only unveils a previously overlooked dynamic instability mechanism in buckling-based materials, but also provides an analytical framework for predicting and designing auxetic rotating polygonal metamaterials, with implications for future applications in vibration control and soft robotics.

title: A cointegration-driven auto-adaptive neural network strategy for strain-based structural health monitoring of masonry structures and its application for damage detection in full-scale experimental testing
abstract: Strain is a highly effective damage-sensitive feature for Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) of masonry structures. However, Environmental and Operational Variations (EOVs), such as air temperature changes, can induce drifts in strain time series that mask damage-related patterns, requiring compensatory techniques for reliable novelty detection. This paper proposes a cointegration-driven, auto-adaptive neural network strategy for strain-based SHM in masonry structures, a field where effective approaches remain limited. The methodology integrates nonlinear cointegration principles with a customized Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) regressor at the sensor level. Unlike standard implementations, the MLP captures time dependency through a modified input matrix that incorporates historical information, enabling damage-sensitive features cleansed of EOV effects. Novelty analysis then combines stationarity assessment with statistically robust control charts for damage detection. A Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) validates the proposed time-dependent MLP model, and a Convolutional Autoencoder (CAE) is adopted as a benchmark to assess novelty detection against an established deep-learning paradigm. A case study consisting of a full-scale masonry building monitored through smart bricks and subjected to varying damage scenarios under real environmental conditions demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed strategy. Results show that the time-dependent MLP achieves higher computational efficiency than the RNN while maintaining accuracy, that the nonlinear cointegration approach overcomes key limitations of linear methods in EOV compensation and damage detection, and that the proposed framework matches the CAE in novelty detection at a markedly lower computational cost. Overall, this supports a broader and more effective application of strain-based SHM in masonry structures.

A broadband piezoelectric-electromagnetic hybrid energy harvester based on a multi-magnetic coupling structure
abstract: This paper introduces a broadband piezoelectric-electromagnetic hybrid energy harvester based on a multi-magnetic coupling structure. This research conducts theoretical analysis and performance evaluation of this energy harvester. The test experiments adopt the variable-control method. In this experiment, the parameters of the magnetic coupling and limiters were changed to explore the output performance of this energy harvester. The test results show that by adjusting the magnetic coupling parameters, the bandwidth of this energy harvester is increased from 4 Hz to 9.5 Hz. Compared with the piezoelectric energy harvester without magnetic coupling, the bandwidth of this energy harvester has increased by 171.4%. By changing the parameters of the limiters, the maximum peak-to-peak voltage generated by this energy harvester is increased from 22 V to 27.6 V. In addition, with an external load of 16 KΩ, the maximum root mean square power of this energy harvester is 13.1 mW. Application experiments prove that this energy harvester can continuously power 80 LED lights or an electronic thermometer. This shows that the output performance of the energy harvester proposed in this paper can meet the power supply needs of some low-power devices.

Experimental identification of a bistable device for seismic energy dissipation
abstract: This work describes a novel method for experimentally measuring and identifying dynamic parameters of bistable systems. The investigated samples are physical models of unit cells of mechanical metamaterials used for seismic energy dissipation. In order to identify this type of nonlinear systems, the paper proposes a new instantaneous probabilistic algorithm, which is capable of extracting the causal components of the dynamic response from the random ones. This is especially relevant for nonlinear systems exhibiting abrupt transitions between dynamical regimes, whose frequency content can evolve significantly over time. In particular, the approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) approach is extended to the time-frequency representation of non-stationary dynamic responses typical of bistable systems. The method was tested on experimental measurements of 3D-printed bistable samples with the final goal of estimating the instantaneous energy dissipated under different external excitations, proving the device's effectiveness.

Data-informed simulation of temperature effects in finite element models for structural health monitoring using inverse surrogate modeling
abstract: This work presents a data-informed framework to simulate temperature effects in a finite element model (FEM) for structural health monitoring (SHM), enabling realistic generation of synthetic modal data for both healthy and damaged states. A challenge in vibration-based SHM is that real damaged data are rarely available, so damage detection and classification methods are often validated using FEM simulations. However, temperature strongly affects modal data through changes in stiffness, connections, and boundary conditions, and these effects are difficult to reproduce realistically using standard thermo-mechanical assumptions, especially when only few temperature measurements are available. The proposed approach combines field monitoring data with an updated FEM through inverse surrogate modeling. First, an inverse surrogate model is trained on FEM simulations to recover temperature-sensitive mechanical parameters (e.g., Young’s modulus of elasticity) from modal frequencies. Then, this surrogate is applied to long-term monitoring data to estimate how these parameters evolve with temperature. A second regression model then learns a direct mapping from temperature to FEM parameters. Injecting these temperature-dependent parameters into the FEM allows simulation of realistic temperature-frequency trends, for both healthy and damage scenarios. The method is demonstrated on a numerical truss and on the KW51 railway bridge. Results show high accuracy in modal frequency prediction and consistent anomaly detection performance, indicating that the framework reproduces in-situ thermal effects without requiring explicit thermo-mechanical modeling, while preserving damage detectability under temperature variations.

Upper approximation bounds for neural oscillators
abstract: Neural oscillators, originating from second-order ordinary differential equations (ODEs), have demonstrated strong performance in stably learning causal mappings between long-term sequences or continuous temporal functions, as well as in accurately approximating physical systems. However, theoretically quantifying the capacities of their neural network architectures remains a significant challenge. In this study, the neural oscillator consisting of a second-order ODE followed by a multilayer perceptron (MLP) is considered. Its upper approximation bound for approximating causal and uniformly continuous operators between continuous temporal function spaces and that for approximating uniformly asymptotically incrementally stable second-order dynamical systems are derived. The established proof method of the approximation bound for approximating the causal continuous operators can also be directly applied to state-space models consisting of a linear time-continuous complex recurrent neural network followed by an MLP. Theoretical results reveal that the approximation error of the neural oscillator for approximating the second-order dynamical systems scales polynomially with the reciprocals of the widths of two utilized MLPs, thus overcoming the curse of parametric complexity. The convergence rates of two established approximation error bounds are validated through four numerical cases. These results provide a robust theoretical foundation for the effective application of the neural oscillator in science and engineering.

title: Interpretable physics-guided modelling and energy-efficient disturbance-compensated control for magnetorheological suspensions of off-road vehicles
abstract: Magnetorheological (MR) dampers are widely recognized as an effective solution for vibration attenuation in off-road vehicles, while their inherent nonlinearity and hysteresis pose a significant challenge for precise force tracking and real-time control. To address this problem, this paper proposes a novel control framework that integrates a Physics-Guided Differentiable Optimization-based Inverse Model (PG-DOIM) within a composite Active Disturbance Rejection Control (ADRC) architecture for the control of MR suspension. Initially, a modified Bouc-Wen forward model is identified based on the dynamic test data to characterize the intrinsic properties of the damper. Unlike conventional black-box data-driven approaches, the proposed PG-DOIM reformulates force tracking as a regularized differentiable optimization layer that calculates the required command voltage. This inverse solver is embedded in a composite ADRC control architecture, augmented by an extended state observer and an energy-efficient event-triggering mechanism to compensate for modelling error and external disturbances. Quarter-car simulations and on-road experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms other representative control strategies in suppressing body acceleration and decreasing suspension deflection. Notably, the introduction of the event-triggering mechanism reduces the control update frequency by 46.4% while maintaining comparable vibration isolation performance. Further analyses of power spectral density demonstrate a substantial reduction of vibration energy within human-sensitive frequency ranges, leading to improved ride comfort for passengers.

Compound elastic concentrator for achromatic superfocusing and amplified energy harvesting over an ultra-broadband spectrum
abstract: Elastic metasurfaces offer a compact route to manipulate wavefronts, yet their focusing performance is intrinsically chromatic because the retarded phase varies strongly with operating frequency. This spectral dispersion induces chromatic aberration and deteriorates energy capture, which limits ultra-broadband elastic-wave concentration and reliable piezoelectric energy harvesting in practical plate-based systems. Here, we propose and demonstrate a compound elastic concentrator that integrates a thickness-programmed elastic metasurface with a conformally mapped gradient-index concentrator, enabling achromatic superfocusing over an ultra-broadband spectrum. A central advance is a unified, analytically tractable unit-cell platform grounded in Reissner–Mindlin plate theory, which allows both components to be designed and fabricated by modulating only the local plate thickness. In this two-stage architecture, the metasurface provides high numerical aperture steering and compact pre-focusing, while the gradient-index concentrator continuously recaptures and confines the diffracted waves, thereby suppressing the chromatic aberration inherent to elastic metasurfaces. Numerical and experimental validations verify diffraction-limited, frequency-stable superfocusing in the compound elastic concentrator over the 40–100 kHz operating band, together with substantial intensity enhancement compared with standalone configurations. When a piezoelectric energy harvester is positioned at the confocal hotspot, the concentrated elastic-wave energy converts efficiently into electrical output, yielding markedly enhanced output power across the operating band. These results establish a design- and fabrication-friendly, thickness-only pathway toward ultra-broadband elastic-wave concentration for self-powered sensing, structural health monitoring, and vibration-energy harvesting.

Sensor fusion for track geometry monitoring: integrating on-board condition monitoring and degradation models via Kalman filtering
abstract: Track geometry monitoring is essential for maintaining the safety and efficiency of railway operations. While Track Recording Cars (TRCs) provide accurate measurements of track geometry indicators, their limited availability and high operational costs restrict frequent monitoring across large rail networks. Recent advancements in on-board sensor systems installed on in-service trains offer a cost-effective alternative by enabling high-frequency, albeit less accurate, data collection. This study proposes a method to enhance the reliability of track geometry predictions by integrating low-accuracy sensor vibration signals with degradation models through a Kalman filter framework. An experimental campaign using a low-cost sensor system mounted on a TRC evaluates the proposed approach. The results demonstrate that incorporating frequent sensor data significantly reduces prediction uncertainty, even when the data is noisy. The study also investigates how the frequency of data recording influences the size of the credible prediction interval, providing guidance on the optimal deployment of on-board sensors for effective track monitoring and maintenance planning.

Resonator-based mass density identification in nanoplates
abstract: In this paper, we present a methodological and computational study of an inverse eigenvalue problem with finite data arising from the determination of a distributed mass added to a uniform rectangular nanoplate acting as a mass resonator. The nanoplate is modeled within a simplified strain-gradient theory in linear elasticity, under the Kirchhoff–Love kinematic assumptions and with simply supported boundary conditions. The identification method relies on the lowest (Formula presented) eigenvalues and is based on an iterative procedure that approximates the unknown mass density by means of a truncated generalized Fourier series computed on a specific family of test functions. The added mass is assumed to be small compared to the total mass, and its support is confined to a quarter of the rectangular domain. Numerical simulations show that the reconstruction of smooth mass distributions with connected support of diameter larger that (Formula presented) the average side of the nanoplate domain is quite accurate, even when the mass perturbation is not necessarily small. The identification of discontinuous mass densities is less accurate, and a Gibbs-like phenomenon occurs near the jumps. The accuracy of the reconstruction degrades progressively as the number of the connected components of the added mass support increases. Numerical tests show that the identification method remains stable in the presence of errors on the data, provided that such errors are, on average, significantly smaller than the natural frequency-changes induced by the added mass.

Operational modal analysis of a rotating blade using continuously scanning laser Doppler vibrometer measurements
abstract: Operational modal analysis (OMA) is a powerful technique for identifying the dynamic characteristics of rotating blades under operating conditions. One limitation of standard OMA approaches, however, is that linear time invariance is assumed, which is not the case for wind turbines with rotating blades. Traditional vibration measurement techniques face limitations due to the challenges of capturing high-resolution modal data on rotating blades and possibly not detecting problems in all parts of the blade. This paper presents an extended harmonic power spectrum method for OMA using a continuously tracking and scanning laser Doppler vibrometer (CTSLDV) system, which enables measuring with a wind turbine in operation. A test rig with a small wind turbine is used in this work to evaluate the proposed measurement and analysis methods. The CTSLDV system continuously scans on the central axis of the blade under operational conditions and the mode shapes are successfully estimated using different scan frequencies. The results highlight the advantages of using a continuous scanning and extended harmonic power spectrum method for full-field vibration analysis of the linear time-periodic systems, which can enhance structural health monitoring and predictive maintenance of rotating machinery under operational conditions.

CS-SHAP: Extending SHAP to cyclic-spectral domain for better interpretability of intelligent fault diagnosis
abstract: Neural networks (NNs), with their powerful nonlinear mapping and end-to-end capabilities, are widely applied in mechanical intelligent fault diagnosis (IFD). However, as typical black-box models, they pose challenges in understanding their decision basis and logic, limiting their deployment in high-reliability scenarios. Hence, various methods have been proposed to enhance the interpretability of IFD. Among these, post-hoc approaches can provide explanations without changing model architecture, preserving its flexibility and scalability. However, existing post-hoc methods often suffer from limitations in explanation forms. They either require preprocessing that disrupts the end-to-end nature or overlook fault mechanisms, leading to suboptimal explanations. To address these issues, we derived the cyclic-spectral (CS) transform and proposed the CS-SHAP by extending Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) to the CS domain. CS-SHAP can evaluate contributions from both carrier and modulation frequencies, aligning more closely with fault mechanisms and delivering clearer and more accurate explanations. Three datasets are utilized to validate the superior interpretability of CS-SHAP, ensuring its correctness, reproducibility, and practical performance. With open-source code and outstanding interpretability, CS-SHAP has the potential to be widely adopted and become the post-hoc interpretability benchmark in IFD, even in other classification tasks. The code is available on https://github.com/ChenQian0618/CS-SHAP.

Passive elastic mode-resolver with dispersion-engineered metasurfaces
abstract: Intrinsic modal dispersion confines most elastic metasurfaces to a single encoded functionality, and mode-resolved analysis of plate-guided waves therefore still relies on bulky transducers or extensive signal postprocessing. Here, we introduce a passive elastic mode-resolver for Lamb-wave identification based on a frequency-specific dispersion-engineered metasurface. A birefringent meta-atom is designed to exhibit pronounced mode-dependent dispersion, and its dynamic behavior is systematically characterized through eigenanalysis. By leveraging the fabrication flexibility of elastic metasurfaces, the required meta-atoms can be arranged without relying on extensive meta-atom libraries or computationally intensive optimization. Designed to operate at a specific frequency of 100 kHz, the proposed metasurface selectively focuses incident S0 and A0 modes to spatially encoded positions, thereby enabling identification of the propagating mode from the resulting intensity distribution. By integrating a piezoelectric element at each encoded focal position, the mechanically concentrated wave energy is converted into a mode-dependent electrical signal, enabling passive electrical readout of the encoded modal response. As a result, the mode-resolver provides a compact and passive alternative to bulkier systems conventionally used in structural health monitoring, ultrasonic sensing, and related industrial applications. By independently processing mode-dependent information within a single passive platform, it offers a practical route toward expanded mechanical functionality in transportation infrastructure, large civil structures, and smart facilities.

Misalignment safety threshold and stability driven controller tuning for AMBs–rotor systems
abstract: Active magnetic bearings (AMBs)–rotor systems are widely used in high precision machinery and energy equipment due to their contactless support capability. In these systems, coupling misalignment caused by manufacturing, assembly, or wear can induce asymmetric forces, leading to excessive rotor vibrations and decreased stability. Although controller parameter tuning methods are commonly based on empirical rules, classical control design, or numerical optimization, most existing approaches focus on conventional performance indices. They rarely consider coupling misalignment tolerance as an explicit design objective, making it difficult to guarantee system robustness and safety under varying misalignment conditions. Herein, a controller parameter tuning method based on both the misalignment safety threshold and system stability constraints is proposed. Specifically, the misalignment safety threshold is defined by the allowable misalignment area from the nonlinear electromechanical model of the AMBs–rotor system with coupling misalignment, while system stability is evaluated through root locus analysis. Simulation and experimental verifications under coupling misalignments are conducted. This method maximizes the system’s tolerance to coupling misalignment while maintaining stability margins and introduces a novel criterion for tuning controller parameters in AMBs–rotor systems.

abstract: A novel physics-guided machine learning framework is proposed for the numerical simulation of complex nonlinear behaviors and to improve the generalization capability of data-driven models under limited information conditions. It combines an a priori physics-based model with a new neural network (NN) architecture designed to compensate for its inaccuracies. A differential evolution algorithm is adopted for the parametric identification of the physics-based model. On the other hand, an original transformer-based NN, enhanced with a long short-term memory (LSTM) feature fusion layer, is employed to capture the inherent aspects of the nonlinear behavior that are overlooked by the physics-based model so as to reduce overall errors.This approach is applied to simulate the hysteretic tensile behavior of NiTiNOL shape memory alloy wires subject to different loading rates. A comprehensive experimental comparative assessment is carried out between a physics-based (phenomenological) model and four NN architectures, including the uni- and bi-directional LSTM models, a transformer model, as well as the proposed model merging LSTM and transformer components. These NN architectures are employed both in a fully data-driven setting and within the physics-guided framework herein conceived with the purpose of mitigating the inaccuracies arising from the selected phenomenological model.The results indicate that the proposed NN architecture connecting LSTM and transformer components achieves the best overall performance. Furthermore, the physics-guided approach consistently improves both accuracy and reliability of the predictions.

Experimentally validated reconfigurable piezoelectric metamaterial plate for sound directivity control
abstract: This work presents an experimentally validated investigation of a reconfigurable piezoelectric metamaterial plate designed for sound directivity control. The metastructure consists of an aluminum plate with an array of piezoelectric patches, each connected to a tunable resonant shunt circuit. By selectively adjusting the spatial distribution of tuned and open-circuit elements, it becomes possible to modify vibration modes and steer the radiated acoustic energy without physically modifying the structure. The study presents transverse velocity and near-field acoustic measurements of the metastructure, which also validate the finite element simulations of the vibroacoustic system. Results demonstrate that different tuning patterns can confine vibrations to specific regions of the plate, producing far-field radiation patterns that range from omnidirectional to highly directional lobes. These findings emphasize the potential of reconfigurable piezoelectric metamaterials as a versatile solution for adaptive noise and vibration control in engineering applications.

Creating a smooth and wide attenuation band in the transmissibility of beam vibration using a neutraliser
abstract: This paper investigates how a single vibration neutraliser can be attached to a beam to create a wide frequency range in which vibration transmission is reduced. This range, termed the smooth wide attenuation band (WAB), is defined as the region where the displacement transmissibility across the beam is below unity and exhibits no peaks or troughs. The concept is motivated by similar behaviour observed in mono-coupled periodic rods. The primary aim of the study is to identify the physical mechanisms responsible for the formation of the WAB and to establish an effective approach for tuning the neutraliser. Using the receptance method, with the beam modelled using its vibration modes, it is shown that the formation of a WAB requires specific conditions. The neutraliser must be placed at a nodal point of the beam and be tuned such that the real part of its dynamic stiffness is equal and opposite to the mass-like receptance of the beam at the corresponding natural frequency. The analysis shows that the WAB results from a degenerate mode condition in which two vibration modes of the combined beam–neutraliser system coincide in frequency. Numerical simulations indicate that attaching the neutraliser at the nodal point nearest to the end of the beam which is excited, produces a wider WAB and greater reduction in transmissibility than using the nodal point near the opposite end. These findings, which are supported by experimental validation, provide new physical insight into the WAB phenomenon on a beam.

Approximation of structural intensity from experimental structural response data using a hybrid method − methodology, verification, and validation
abstract: Structural intensity is a response quantity that allows visualization and quantification of the vibrational power flow in structures. Numerical simulations allow for easy calculation, i.e., by combining standard result datasets of finite element analysis. However, this is not the case for experimental data, where usually an incomplete set of response quantities (i.e., just translational responses) of a subset of the degrees of freedom of the corresponding finite element model serves as the fundamental dataset to compute the structural intensity. This paper provides a comprehensive guide for a hybrid method that allows the calculation of structural intensity on arbitrary surfaces in three-dimensional space. The hybrid method utilizes experimentally acquired structural response data as an input. The corresponding measurement point locations build a mesh with associated trial functions. Furthermore, we verify the methodology utilizing numerical data to quantify the method's accuracy. Moreover, comparing structural intensity fields acquired from a numerical model and measurement data helps to validate the proposed approach further. Finally, the methodology supports engineers in utilizing the concept of structural intensity to optimize mechanical systems in terms of structural dynamics, e.g., the smart application of damping elements to control system dynamics efficiently.

Measurement of high-frequency vibration modes using event cameras and low-rank tensor completion
abstract: Various optical methods have been developed to visualize and measure dynamic structural behaviors, such as vibration modes and frequency spectra, for detecting fastener loosening and crack propagation. However, capturing high-frequency vibration modes typically requires high-speed cameras, which involve substantial power consumption, data volume, and cost. This study addresses these challenges by introducing a vibration measurement method based on an event camera, which records only logarithmic changes in luminance, combined with rectangular tracking and low-rank tensor completion for displacement reconstruction. The proposed method was experimentally validated through vibration measurements of a 630-mm-long polyvinyl chloride pipe and a coil spring. The results demonstrated that the method can quantitatively measure displacement waveforms under single-frequency, multi-frequency, and band-limited noise excitation conditions. For the pipe vibration tests, the normalized mean squared error (MSE) of the measured displacement waveform was less than 3% at relatively large displacement amplitudes of approximately 0.5 pixels, corresponding to 0.25 mm. Even at smaller amplitudes of approximately 0.1 pixels, corresponding to 0.05 mm, the MSE remained below 25%, demonstrating that the proposed method can quantitatively measure subpixel vibrations. The vibration modes exhibited a modal assurance criterion ≥ 0.9 under all test conditions, demonstrating excellent agreement with finite-element method results. Additionally, the proposed approach successfully detected changes in vibration modes caused by loosened bolted joints. The upper frequency measurement limit was assessed using an ultrasonic transducer experiment, achieving quantitative displacement spectrum measurements at a vibration frequency of 19.75 kHz and amplitudes of 30.1–37.6 μm. The mean MSE was below 10% for frequencies above 1 kHz. However, since ultrasonic vibrations are extremely subtle, it is necessary to zoom in significantly to capture them, and we have not yet been able to measure the vibration modes; this will be a topic for future research.

A long-stroke fast tool servo system equipped with floating stator and its application in ultra-precision machining
abstract: Long-stroke fast tool servo (FTS) systems have been widely applied to the machining of freeform surfaces. However, the inertial force generated by long-stroke motion still constitutes a key bottleneck restricting the improvement of machining accuracy for such systems. In this paper, a balanced long-stroke fast tool servo (BFTS) system integrated with a voice coil motor (VCM), an aerostatic guideway and an inertial balancing device is designed. Aiming at the conventional mounting scheme in which the VCM of traditional FTS systems is fixed on the machine tool, this study proposes a structural improvement scheme featuring a floating stator, drawing on the flexible tool-tip guiding design concept of FTS. Two rectangular thin plates are employed to suspend the stator of the VCM, thereby realizing the balancing of inertial forces.This study adopted a combined method of theoretical calculation, finite element analysis, and experimental verification to systematically investigate the influence laws of the stiffness of rectangular thin plates, the mass of the counterweight system, and the operating frequency of the BFTS on the inertial force attenuation effect. Theoretical analysis and experimental test results show that when the operating frequency of the BFTS is 30 Hz, the inertial force output by the VCM decreases from 10 N to less than 1 N.Experiments confirm that the inertial balancing system does not affect the system bandwidth. Moreover, the thrust ripple of the VCM introduced by the inertial balancing system is negligible. Finally, inclined surface turning experiments confirm that the proposed inertial balancing system can significantly improve the surface quality of machined workpieces. The system can meet the precision requirements for the ultra-precision machining of optical components with high aspect ratios.keywords:Fast tool servo; Counterbalance ; Rectangular thin plate ; Inertial balance ; Finite element analysis

Sensor informativeness, identifiability, and uncertainty in Bayesian inverse problems for structural health monitoring
abstract: In Structural Health Monitoring (SHM), the recovery of distributed mechanical parameters from sparse data is often ill-posed, raising critical questions about identifiability and the reliability of inferred states. While deterministic regularization methods such as Tikhonov stabilise the inversion, they provide little insight into the spatial limits of resolution or the inherent uncertainty of the solution. This paper presents a Bayesian inverse framework that rigorously quantifies these limits, using the identification of distributed flexural rigidity from rotation (tilt) influence lines as a primary case study. Fisher information is employed as a diagnostic metric to quantify sensor informativeness, revealing how specific sensor layouts and load paths constrain the recoverable spatial features of the parameter field. The methodology is applied to the full-scale openLAB research bridge (TU Dresden) using data from controlled vehicle passages. Beyond estimating the flexural rigidity profile, the Bayesian formulation produces credible intervals that expose regions of practical non-identifiability, which deterministic methods may obscure. The results demonstrate that while the measurement data carry high information content for the target parameters, their utility is spatially heterogeneous and strictly bounded by the experiment design. The proposed framework unifies identification with uncertainty quantification, providing a rigorous basis for optimising sensor placement and interpreting the credibility of SHM diagnostics.

A physics-informed dual-stream convolutional neural network method for in-situ continuous bolt preload monitoring and detection
abstract: Accurate perception of bolt preload is crucial for ensuring the reliability and safety of critical equipment such as aero-engines, high-speed trains, and wind turbines. To address the limitations of existing data-driven methods, including poor interpretability, heavy reliance on labeled data, and weak out-of-distribution generalization, this paper proposes a Physics-informed Dual-stream Convolutional Neural Network (PI-CNN) method for bolt preload detection. The core of the method lies in embedding the experimentally verified linear physical relationship between the square of natural frequency of bolt vibration and the preload into the neural network training process in the form of a gradient consistency loss. The model adopts a dual-channel 1D-CNN architecture to extract features from the raw vibration acceleration signals and their frequency spectra separately. It then incorporates handcrafted feature, specifically the squared natural frequency, to construct a data-physics dual-driven loss function. This design constrains the model predictions not only to fit the data but also to strictly adhere to known physical law, thereby significantly enhancing the physical interpretability of the model. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method, guided by physical principles, markedly improves model interpretability, reduces dependency on labeled data, and enhances generalization performance under unseen working conditions, offering an efficient data-physics dual-driven solution for bolt preload detection.

Beyond static models: Hypernetworks for adaptive and generalizable forecasting in complex parametric dynamical systems
abstract: Dynamical systems play a key role in modeling, forecasting, and decision-making across a wide range of scientific domains. However, variations in system parameters, also referred to as parametric variability, can lead to drastically different model behavior and output, posing challenges for constructing models that generalize across parameter regimes. In this work, we introduce the Parametric Hypernetwork for Learning Interpolated Networks (PHLieNet), a framework that simultaneously learns: (a) a global mapping from the parameter space to a nonlinear embedding and (b) a mapping from the inferred embedding to the weights of a dynamics propagation network. The learned embedding serves as a latent representation that modulates a base network, termed the hypernetwork , enabling it to generate the weights of a target network responsible for forecasting the system’s state evolution conditioned on the previous time history. By interpolating in the space of models rather than observations, PHLieNet facilitates smooth transitions across parameterized system behaviors, enabling a unified model that captures the dynamic behavior across a broad range of system parameterizations. The performance of the proposed technique is validated in a series of dynamical systems with respect to its ability to extrapolate in time and interpolate and extrapolate in the parameter space, i.e., generalize to dynamics that were unseen during training. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both short-term forecast accuracy and in capturing long-term dynamical features such as attractor statistics.

title: Towards a more realistic evaluation of machine learning models for bearing fault diagnosis
abstract: Reliable detection of bearing faults is essential for maintaining the safety and operational efficiency of rotating machinery. While recent advances in machine learning (ML), particularly deep learning, have shown strong performance in controlled settings, many studies fail to generalize to real-world applications due to methodological flaws, most notably data leakage. This paper investigates the issue of data leakage in vibration-based bearing fault diagnosis and its impact on model evaluation. We demonstrate that common dataset partitioning strategies, such as segment-wise and condition-wise splits, introduce spurious correlations that inflate performance metrics. To address this, we propose a rigorous, leakage-free evaluation methodology centered on bearing-wise data partitioning, ensuring no overlap between the physical components used for training and testing. Additionally, we reformulate the classification task as a multi-label problem, enabling the detection of co-occurring fault types and the use of prevalence-independent metrics based on the ROC curve. Beyond preventing leakage, we also examine the effect of dataset diversity on generalization, showing that the number of unique training bearings is a decisive factor for achieving robust performance. We evaluate our methodology on four widely adopted datasets: Case Western Reserve University (CWRU), Paderborn University (PU), University of Ottawa (UORED-VAFCLS) and Hanoi University of Science and Technology (HUST bearing). This study highlights the importance of leakage-aware evaluation protocols and provides practical guidelines for dataset partitioning, model selection, and validation, fostering the development of more trustworthy ML systems for industrial fault diagnosis applications.

title: BiMSFNet: A binarized multi-scale feature fusion network for privacy-preserving enhanced diagnosis on edge devices
abstract: Rotating machinery is critical equipment in modern industry, and the health status of its bearings directly affects system safety and efficiency. Due to the complexity of the deep learning diagnostic model and the large number of parameters, it is difficult to deploy it in resource-constrained edge embedded devices in real time, and there is also a risk of data privacy leakage. To address these issues, this paper proposes a Binarized Multi-Scale Feature Fusion Network (BiMSFNet) for edge embedded devices. First, in data preprocessing, quantization and bit-plane decomposition convert 2D time–frequency maps into multi-dimensional binary matrices, achieving information transformation and initial privacy protection. Moreover, by leveraging the inherent discretization and non-continuity of the binary neural network itself further resist gradient inversion attacks at the model level. Then, by combining binary neural networks with adaptive weighting, a lightweight model is constructed. Finally, integrating multi-dilation-rate convolutions with adaptive weighting enables multi-scale feature extraction while drastically reducing model size and training cost. Experiments show that BiMSFNet achieves 99.54% average accuracy on a self-built testbed and 99.18% on the SEU bearing dataset with only 0.169M parameters and 17.6MFLOPs, 1–2 orders of magnitude lower than mainstream lightweight models, and effectively resists gradient inversion attacks on the CWRU dataset. Deployed on a Raspberry Pi 5B, inference time is 2.8ms per sample, meeting the real-time, low-power, and privacy requirements of edge scenarios.

title: Extreme reciprocal asymmetric elastic wave energy transport enabled by an ultra-thin, non-deflecting Willis structure
abstract: Signal rectification protects sensor systems that are vulnerable to external disturbances and enables diode-based signal control. Achieving such direction-dependent energy transport, however, typically requires breaking reciprocity through cumbersome devices, which limits practical feasibility. In addition, metamaterial- or diffraction-based approaches often rely on bulky structures or deflect the wave propagation direction, with wave deflection compromising signal fidelity. Therefore, realizing strong asymmetric energy transport in a compact, non-deflecting, and reciprocal device remains elusive. Here, we present a subwavelength mode-coupled Willis-type structure that enables highly asymmetric elastic wave transmission by fundamentally engineering the elastic constitutive relations. By identifying and enhancing the mode coupled Willis coefficients, which are otherwise weak, we establish a systematic route for controlling direction dependent intermodal energy exchange between longitudinal and shear wave modes. Leveraging this mechanism, we demonstrate unidirectional perfect transmission and reflection, in which complete mode converting transmission occurs for one sided incidence while total reflection arises for the opposite direction, all while preserving reciprocity. Ultrasonic experiments in a plate confirm unidirectional perfect mode-converting transmission and reflection for shear-horizontal wave incidence, in good agreement with numerical simulations. Unlike previous approaches, the proposed ultra-thin structure achieves strong asymmetric energy transport while preserving the signal direction and reciprocity, thereby enabling reliable signal communication. As potential applications, we further demonstrate elastic wave diodes and signal isolation, highlighting the practical utility of mode coupled Willis structures for directional wave control.

Recursive Gaussian process state space model
abstract: Learning dynamical models from data is not only fundamental but also holds great promise for advancing principle discovery, time-series prediction, and controller design. Among various approaches, Gaussian Process State-Space Models (GPSSMs) have recently gained significant attention due to their combination of flexibility and interpretability. However, for online learning, the field lacks an efficient method suitable for scenarios where prior information regarding data distribution and model function is limited. To address this issue, this paper proposes a recursive GPSSM method with adaptive capabilities for both operating domains and Gaussian process (GP) hyperparameters. Specifically, we first utilize first-order linearization to derive a Bayesian update equation for the joint distribution between the system state and the GP model, enabling closed-form and domain-independent learning. Second, an online selection algorithm for inducing points is developed based on informative criteria to achieve lightweight learning. Third, to support online hyperparameter optimization, we recover historical measurement information from the current filtering distribution. Comprehensive evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the superior accuracy, computational efficiency, and adaptability of our method compared to state-of-the-art online GPSSM techniques.

New insight into the modelling, identification, and analysis of a hybrid active vibration control of structures
abstract: In the present paper, a new perspective on comprehensive experimental–numerical modelling and identification of active structures is presented. The control object is a flat beam with one piezoelectric actuator and a contact sensor, forming a collocated system, or with three non-contact sensors, such as eddy-current or laser sensors, forming a hybrid non-collocated system. First, an analytical model of an actuator is derived from equilibrium equations. Next, the active beam is modelled analytically and numerically using 1D, 2D, and 3D Finite Element Method to comprehensively analyse the effect of actuator placement on the beam’s modal parameters. In addition to this aim, calibration of the actual industrial actuator and sensor responses was performed to obtain an accurate 3D FEM model of the piezoelectric patches based on the electromechanical coupling. The obtained active beam models are calibrated using experimental results for active beam vibration excited by a modal hammer impact and by a continuous chirp function generated by the actuator. An analytical model of the actuator, combined with finite-element and experimental results, enabled us to define optimal and quasi-optimal control forces and actuator placement that satisfy two proposed force- and energy-quality indicators. In addition, the effect of actuator length on modal frequencies, forces, energies, masses, and stiffness is examined in depth. Finally, the ARX identification procedure is applied to time-dependent experimental and 3D FEM numerical vibrational responses of the beam to obtain discrete and continuous single-input triple-output (SITO) state-space models with the maximum reduced order for the first three/four resonances. At the end, the impulse responses and stability of the ARX discrete and continuous models were shown in the time and frequency domains to demonstrate their correctness and accuracy. The proposed design methodology of the active control structure may be applied to both classical and composite structures. Next, different control laws can be tested in simulation and experiment to confirm the proposed design methodology of the active system.

An Integrated novel random decrement technique and system identification framework for modal features extraction in structural health monitoring
abstract: Structural health monitoring (SHM) techniques are used for monitoring the condition of structures, including bridges, buildings, dams, among others, through data acquired from embedded sensors. An integral aspect of SHM involves feature extraction, wherein algorithms analyze raw sensor data to generate explainable features regarding the health state of structures. The random decrement technique (RDT) is a notable signal processing method used to estimate the free response of mechanical structures, crucial for extracting frequency features related to structural dynamics. However, studies have shown that RDT encounters performance issues in cases of nonlinear damping, significant signal noise, and overlapping vibration modes. In a previous study, a data-driven classifier for transient and stationary regimes in multivariate dynamic systems was introduced, employing differential geometry tools to analyze stochastic properties. In this paper, the authors applied this classifier to develop a novel frequency-feature extraction method for SHM. This method incorporates a modified triggering condition for RDT and a recent system identification technique, aiming to improve frequency-feature estimation, especially in segment selection and modal parameter estimation of free responses in non-linear structures. Validation of the proposed approach employed mechanical vibration data from four accelerometer sensors on the “Andoian DF 12” bridge in Guipuzkoa, Spain, covering a one-year period and providing comprehensive insights into structural dynamics across different seasons. Comparative analysis against traditional RDT and various system identification techniques demonstrated that the proposed methodology improve the estimation of structural free responses by reducing noise and requiring fewer data compared to traditional RDTs. Moreover, the estimated modes aligned with the spectral content of mechanical sensors, indicating suitability for online applications with minimal computational costs and accurate modal parameter estimation for SHM in structures.

Natural gradient active control for coupled vibro-acoustic systems under spatially structured metrics
abstract: Active noise and vibration control (ANVC) in coupled vibro-acoustic systems often suffers from severe convergence imbalance and poor numerical conditioning caused by heterogeneous acoustic and structural channels. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a physically informed adaptive control framework based on a block-diagonal stochastic natural gradient descent (BDSNGD) algorithm. By introducing structured metric preconditioning within a Riemannian metric space, the proposed method effectively aligns the dominant spatial eigenvalues of heterogeneous actuation channels, thereby eliminating convergence disparity without requiring computationally expensive full-rank matrix inversion. Furthermore, to overcome the trade-off between transient convergence speed and steady-state excess mean square error (EMSE), a correlation-driven variable step size (CVSS) strategy is developed. Instead of relying on raw error energy, the step size is regulated using the normalized temporal correlation of residual errors, enabling fast adaptation to structured disturbances while suppressing unnecessary updates under uncorrelated noise and impulsive perturbations. Comprehensive theoretical analyses, numerical simulations, and real-time experimental validations on a multichannel vibro-acoustic platform demonstrate that the proposed CVSS-BDSNGD algorithm achieves rapid, synchronous, and well-balanced convergence across heterogeneous channels, superior steady-state noise reduction, and strong robustness against impulsive disturbances, while maintaining a low computational complexity comparable to the conventional FxLMS algorithm.

title: Real-time monitoring and intelligent decision system with a dual-sensing module for optical lens centering
Multi-modal cross-domain mixed fusion model with dual disentanglement for fault diagnosis under unseen working conditions
abstract: Intelligent fault diagnosis has become an indispensable technique for ensuring machinery reliability. However, existing methods suffer significant performance decline in real-world scenarios where models are tested under unseen working conditions, while domain adaptation approaches are limited to their reliance on target domain samples. Moreover, most existing studies rely on single-modal sensing signals, overlooking the complementary nature of multi-modal information for improving model generalization. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a multi-modal cross-domain mixed fusion model with dual disentanglement for fault diagnosis. A dual disentanglement framework is developed to decouple modality-invariant and modality-specific features, as well as domain-invariant and domain-specific representations, enabling both comprehensive multi-modal representation learning and robust domain generalization. A cross-domain mixed fusion strategy is designed to randomly mix modality information across domains for modality and domain diversity augmentation. Furthermore, a triple-modal fusion mechanism is introduced to adaptively integrate multi-modal heterogeneous information. Extensive experiments are conducted on induction motor fault diagnosis under both unseen constant and time-varying working conditions. The results demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms advanced methods and comprehensive ablation studies further verify the effectiveness of each proposed component and multi-modal fusion. The code is available at: https://github.com/xiapc1996/MMDG.

title: Mechanics-informed full-field deformation identification of flexure-dominated high-rise buildings using sparse inclinometer data
abstract: Abstract Structural deformation is a critical indicator of the safety and performance of high-rise buildings. Accurate deformation identification not only provides essential insights into structural behavior but also informs effective maintenance strategies. However, due to sensor limitations and cost constraints, full-field and full-band structural deformation identification remains a significant challenge in current monitoring practices. This study introduces a novel spatiotemporal framework for reconstructing deformations in flexural-dominated high-rise buildings by fusing multisensor data with a deep learning–based model. A system-level dynamic rotation field is first reconstructed from sparse inclinometer data using a physical-enhanced adjacency matrix and is subsequently calibrated with limited accelerometer measurements. The complete deformation field is obtained by superimposing the quasi-static and calibrated dynamic components. Numerical investigations demonstrate the feasibility and robustness of the proposed framework, even under severe sensor sparsity and sensor noise, while maintaining high accuracy in full-field and full-band deformation reconstruction. Comparative studies further indicate that the proposed strategy effectively enhances capability of current deep learning (DL) model for inferring unobserved nodes responses. Real-world validation using data from a super-high-rise building under strong wind and earthquake excitations confirmed the applicability of the method, with results showing good agreement with Global Positioning System (GPS) measurements. The findings also highlight the importance of incorporating full-band responses for reliable assessment, particularly for drift-sensitive components, underscoring the practical potential of the proposed framework.

title: A domain knowledge informed approach for anomaly detection of electric vehicle interior sounds
abstract: The detection of anomalies in automotive cabin sounds is critical for ensuring vehicle quality and maintaining passenger comfort. In many real-world settings, this task is more appropriately framed as an unsupervised learning problem rather than the supervised case due to the scarcity or complete absence of labeled faulty data. In such an unsupervised setting, the model is trained exclusively on healthy samples and detects anomalies as deviations from normal behavior. However, in the absence of labeled faulty samples for validation and the limited reliability of commonly used metrics, such as validation reconstruction error, effective model selection remains a significant challenge. To overcome these limitations, a domain-knowledge-informed approach for model selection is proposed, in which proxy-anomalies engineered through structured perturbations of healthy spectrograms are used in the validation set to support model selection. The proposed methodology is evaluated on a high-fidelity electric vehicle dataset comprising healthy and faulty cabin sounds across five representative fault types viz., Imbalance, Modulation, Whine, Wind, and Pulse Width Modulation. This dataset, generated using advanced sound synthesis techniques, and validated via expert jury assessments, has been made publicly available to facilitate further research. Experimental evaluations on the five fault cases demonstrate the selection of optimal models using proxy-anomalies, significantly outperform conventional model selection strategies.

title: A generalization of the Whittaker–Shannon interpolation formula for non-bandlimited signals
abstract: Reconstructing continuous signals from discrete samples is a fundamental task in interpolation theory. Under ideal assumptions, the classical Whittaker–Shannon interpolation formula guarantees perfect reconstruction for bandlimited signals sampled at the Nyquist rate. However, many real-world systems, particularly sampled-data systems, produce non-bandlimited signals whose intersample behavior is governed by the continuous-time dynamics encoded in the system model, making classical bandlimited reconstruction methods inappropriate. This paper presents a generalized interpolation framework that reconstructs continuous-time outputs from their samples using a model-induced kernel, thereby extending Shannon’s formula to a broader class of signals. The proposed method derives the interpolation kernel from the governing equations of the underlying system, enabling accurate reconstruction of intersample content. Numerical simulations and laboratory experiments on a permanent magnet synchronous machine (PMSM) validate the approach, demonstrating its effectiveness in reconstructing intersample behavior from output samples by leveraging model information.

title: Physics-regularized Bayesian neural network with time-of-arrival refinement for acoustic emission-based damage source localization in concrete beams
abstract: Accurate acoustic emission (AE) source localisation is essential for structural health monitoring (SHM) of concrete structures; however, heterogeneous material properties and complex wave propagation limit the reliability of conventional approaches. This study proposes PR-BNN-ATR, a physics-regularised Bayesian neural network (BNN) with acoustic time-of-arrival refinement for uncertainty-aware AE localisation. Time-difference-of-arrival (TDOA) features extracted using an adaptive Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) picker are used to train a variational BNN, whose hybrid loss combines data fidelity, geometric feasibility, TDOA kinematic consistency, and Kullback–Leibler (KL) regularisation. A deterministic artificial neural network (ANN) and Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout serves as accuracy and uncertainty baselines, respectively. Validated on five notched concrete beams (notch positions 80–40 mm), PR-BNN-ATR achieved mean localisation errors of 3.10–6.19 mm (overall mean 4.04 mm) compared to 1.47–6.58 mm for the ANN. Although the ANN produced lower point errors, PR-BNN-ATR provided calibrated event-wise uncertainty estimates, with Spearman correlation positive for all five beams (ρ = 0.110–0.387), and Mahalanobis joint coverage averaging 91.3% at the 95% nominal level. The variational BNN outperformed MC Dropout on Negative Log-Likelihood in four of five beams. A semi-supervised calibration experiment using a calibration beam b0 with true physical ground-truth coordinates reduced cross-beam error by 82%, confirming genuine localisation learning beyond multilateration replication. Independent digital image correlation (DIC) strain-field measurements confirmed spatial co-localisation of BNN-predicted sources with crack trajectories and linked elevated predictive uncertainty to crack branching, dual crack interaction, and boundary reflection zones, providing non-circular physical validation. These results establish PR-BNN-ATR as an accurate, interpretable, and uncertainty-aware method for risk-informed SHM of concrete structures.

title: Bridging known and unknown: A distribution generation Schrödinger bridge for generalized zero-shot fault diagnosis
A rapid surface roughness evaluation method for single-point diamond turning based on the frequency sensitivity function
Cooperative feature extraction for state monitoring of multiple motors in hub-driven electric vehicles
Regularization strategies of an adaptive active road noise control headrest with the remote microphone technique under head translation
A systematic study of the synergy between passive and active components in a hybrid active–passive sound absorption control system
abstract: Passive sound absorbers, like micro-perforated panels (MPPs) and porous materials, are typically limited in bandwidth or low-frequency performance. Active absorption systems can achieve broadband low-frequency performance but require electrical power and may fail, e.g. during power loss. Hybrid active–passive absorbers therefore offer a promising route to combine the strengths of both approaches. However, existing studies treat the active and passive components independently, without analysing potential synergies that could reduce power demand or ensure sufficient fallback passive performance. This study presents a systematic numerical analysis of a hybrid absorber in a duct, consisting of a porous layer and an elastic MPP driven by an electromagnetic actuator. A feedforward active structural acoustic control strategy is used to actively control sound absorption via the actuated MPP. A regularisation method is introduced to limit actuator electrical power and prevent exceeding the operational constraints. The numerical model is validated through impedance tube measurements and subsequently used to investigate how MPP design parameters (porosity, thickness, hole diameter) and different configurations of the MPP/porous layer arrangement influence both passive and hybrid active–passive absorption. Two design strategies are examined: one with the MPP parameters optimised for maximum passive absorption and one optimised for maximum hybrid performance. The results reveal a fundamental trade-off: designs that maximise hybrid performance reduce passive absorption to improve active control efficiency, while designs prioritising passive performance reduce the effectiveness of the active control. This investigation highlights physical insights that allow effective design of hybrid active–passive systems that could be extended to other similar systems.

title: Hybrid approach for metamaterial behavior prediction for non-uniform resonator grids
abstract: A novel methodology to predict the behavior of metamaterial solutions is presented, with application to a simplified academic structure and an automotive electrical component. In scenarios where a non-uniform grid of resonators is employed, it is essential to consider an alternative to the unit cell modeling strategy, which is typically applied, to ensure robust predictions of metamaterial behavior. In this work, a simulation model of the resonators is combined with experimental transfer functions of the host structure through frequency-based substructuring to obtain these predictions. By employing the recently introduced longest vector approach, the necessity for a substantial number of driving points corresponding to the locations of the resonators, is avoided. Additionally, a metric is proposed to compare various configurations, demonstrating the potential of the presented technique for precise optimizations. The predictions obtained from experimental measurements are compared with those from unit cell modeling. The substructuring methodology offers a robust framework for predicting metamaterial performance in cases where a uniform grid of resonators cannot be placed, or when accurate simulation models of the complex host structure are not readily available.

title: A universal domain adaptation fault diagnosis method based on feature invariance and collaborative mutual learning
Multimodal spatiotemporal graph attention network with uncertainty quantification for aircraft engine prognostics
abstract: Aircraft engine prognostics is critical for safety, cost reduction, and efficient fleet management. Despite the availability of rich multimodal sensor data, most current prognostic approaches are limited to single-modality analysis, lack uncertainty quantification, and rely on predefined sensor graphs. To address these limitations, this paper introduces the Multimodal Spatiotemporal Graph Attention Network with Uncertainty Quantification (MST-GAT-UQ), a novel deep learning framework for aircraft engine prognostics. The proposed model integrates temporal patterns via CNN-LSTM networks, spatial correlations through graph attention mechanisms, and frequency signatures using Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) with 2D CNN processing. Key innovations include a correlation-driven graph construction method that automatically learns sensor relationships from operational data, hierarchical attention fusion to adaptively weight different modalities, and Monte Carlo dropout augmented by temperature scaling for simultaneous Remaining Useful Life (RUL) and health state prediction with calibrated uncertainty intervals. The framework is comprehensively validated on a real-world operational dataset comprising 84 sensors and 43,492 samples from F100-PW-229 turbofan engines, achieving R 2 = 0.911, RMSE = 0.087, MAE = 0.072 on a normalized RUL scale within a synthetic-label verification framework (no ground-truth operational RUL is available for this dataset; reported metrics quantify the model’s fidelity in reproducing a synthetically imposed linear degradation trajectory and should not be interpreted as ground-truth remaining-life predictions), and a synthetic health-state replication accuracy of 99.5% (auxiliary task; health-state labels are a deterministic step-function of the synthetic RUL signal and carry no independent diagnostic information). Comparative analysis against the standard NASA C-MAPSS benchmark is presented as a zero-shot domain-transfer diagnostic, characterising the label-distribution shift between the two datasets, and confirms that native C-MAPSS training yields positive R 2 across all four subsets (FD001–FD004: R 2 = 0.607–0.863). This work represents a significant step toward reliable, uncertainty-aware, and multimodal prognostic systems for safety–critical aviation applications, with uncertainty intervals that are directionally informative but moderately overconfident (empirical coverage 88.7% at the 95% nominal level; ECE = 0.254), indicating that further calibration refinement is required before safety–critical operational deployment.

title: Time-optimal motion trajectory generation incorporating an input shaper for overhead cranes operated by industrial servo systems
abstract: This paper proposes a motion trajectory generation method that achieves time-optimality under input shaping constraints for overhead cranes operated by industrial servo systems. The proposed approach formulates a constrained trajectory optimization problem that minimizes motion time while suppressing residual vibration by embedding a zero-vibration (ZV) or zero-vibration-and-derivative (ZVD) input shaper into the trajectory generation process. By using a simplified model that requires only the natural frequency and damping ratio to characterize vibration, this approach enables practical implementation even when full system identification is difficult. The effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method are demonstrated through simulations and experiments using an overhead crane apparatus. The results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves shorter motion times with effective vibration suppression compared to conventional input shaping and maintains robustness against modeling errors in natural frequency and damping ratio.

title: Adaptive cochlea-simulating acoustic diagnosis method of industrial robot RV reducers
Cross-specification abrasive belt wear monitoring: a physics-informed deep learning framework with acoustic emission burst indicator
abstract: In abrasive belt grinding, switching between belts of differing grit sizes reduces the predictive accuracy of data-driven wear monitoring models. To address this issue, a physics-informed deep learning framework is proposed for continuous abrasive belt wear monitoring across varying belt specifications, in which grinding mechanics are encoded as mechanism-derived input features and physical constraints are embedded in the loss function to guide network learning. An analysis of grain-workpiece contact mechanics reveals that progressive grain dulling shifts the dominant energy dissipation from efficient cutting to parasitic friction. To capture this transition, Acoustic Emission (AE) signals are leveraged, and a novel indicator, the Cumulative Impulse Density–Duration Ratio (CIDDR), is introduced. This metric captures the statistical evolution of AE burst characteristics providing a physically interpretable proxy for the progressive loss of cutting effectiveness. Subsequently, the framework employs a denoising-aware Stacked Sparse Auto-Encoder (SSAE) to extract compact latent representations from these physics-enhanced inputs, followed by a Physics-informed Causal Temporal Convolutional Network (PI-CTCN) regularized by physics-informed loss to ensure physically consistent wear monitoring. To achieve cross-specification generalization, a parameter-based transfer learning strategy adapts the learned representations to belt-induced domain shifts through selective fine-tuning. Experimental validation on two belt specifications (A45 and A160) grinding TC4 titanium alloy demonstrates that the proposed framework achieves an RMSE of 33.54 mg and R² of 0.9857 under cross-belt transfer conditions, reducing RMSE by approximately 20% compared to training from scratch on the target belt, while maintaining stable and continuous wear monitoring.

title: A multi-dimensional rate-independent hysteretic model for homogeneous, isotropic Duhem-like solids
abstract: The class of Duhem-like solids comprises solid bodies composed of rate-independent hysteretic material modeled via a rate-type constitutive equation including the time-derivatives of the stress and strain tensors. To accurately simulate such a complex behavior, a multi-dimensional model is established in the framework of continuum thermodynamics. Particularly, the proposed model is based on three basic assumptions on the size of the deformation (small deformations), the type of material (rate-independent hysteretic material with linear kinematic and/or isotropic hardening), and the properties of the body (homogeneous and isotropic body). Moreover, it requires four material parameters: two govern the rate-independent hysteretic behavior without hardening, whereas the other two control the linear kinematic and isotropic hardening, respectively. A series of simulations are carried out to show the responses provided by the model for different infinitesimal strain histories, hardening conditions, and values of the material parameters. Finally, both numerical and experimental validations are conducted by adopting, in the order, an existing multi-dimensional model and a set of experimental data available in the literature.

title: Fundamental nonlinear mechanisms for vibration energy harvesting: A unified framework for static and time-varying potentials
abstract: Nonlinear vibration energy harvesters based on bistable mechanisms can achieve broadband response and frequency up-conversion, but their performance strongly depends on the underlying dynamical regime and excitation conditions. In this work, two representative architectures are systematically compared: a static-potential energy (SPE) harvester and a time-varying potential energy (TVPE) harvester based on magnetic interactions. A reduced-order nonlinear model with physically consistent parameter sets is developed for both configurations and used to analyze regime activation, frequency response, and load sensitivity. Experimental investigations are conducted to assess qualitative regime consistency and dynamical trends. Results show that SPE devices rely on threshold-driven inter-well activation and exhibit strong sensitivity to excitation amplitude and electrical load, whereas TVPE systems enable robust slow–fast plucking dynamics and effective energy conversion at low-frequency and low-amplitude inputs typical of human motion. Regime transitions and dominant response patterns are consistently reproduced by the model. The proposed comparative framework highlights key dynamical features that can guide the design of nonlinear energy harvesters and vibration control devices.

Data-driven modeling of synthetic wind speed signals with adaptive temporal resolution
abstract: As wind energy systems continue to expand in size and complexity, ensuring their structural reliability under stochastic wind loading has become increasingly critical. Accurate wind speed modeling across multiple temporal scales is essential for reliability assessment, extreme load estimation, and risk-based design. However, a central challenge in data-driven wind speed and storm hazard analysis is the limited temporal resolution of available wind measurements. In practice, wind speed data are often provided as 10 min or hourly averages. While such coarse discretizations are sufficient for estimating aggregate power production, they fail to capture the high-frequency variability that governs extreme loading, structural response, and short-term system dynamics.This paper introduces a novel signal-processing based framework for synthesizing high-resolution wind speed time series from coarse measurements while maintaining statistical and spectral consistency. The methodology operates in the frequency domain, where spectral components are extrapolated and modeled to reflect physically plausible high-frequency behavior while also enforcing a strict energy conservation and preserving extreme-value characteristics.The resulting synthetic wind speed exhibits essential statistical characteristics, including mean values, variance, maximum amplitudes, and distributional properties, this enables high-fidelity stochastic simulations at resolutions suitable for advanced engineering and environmental analyses. The results indicate that the proposed methodology is capable of generating high-resolution, data-informed wind speed realizations with consistent statistical and spectral behavior. The framework provides a robust and computationally efficient tool for wind modeling.

title: A physics-guided evidential multimodal uncertainty framework for small-sample welding defect detection using magneto-optical and infrared imaging
Anti-load performance evaluation method for electro-hydrostatic actuators based on physics-embedded attention mechanism
abstract: High-precision performance degradation evaluation of electro-hydrostatic actuators (EHAs) is critical for aerospace reliability. Among all potential hardware degradation, internal leakage stands out as the most frequent and dominant fault in EHA systems. However, existing methods often fail in dynamic flight environments, where genuine internal leakage signatures are deeply entangled with external variable load disturbances. To address this load-fault coupling challenge, this study proposes an Anti-load Performance Evaluation Method. Firstly, an EHA dynamic model is established to analytically derive a Baseline Contribution Score (BCS), explicitly quantifying the relative sensitivities of multi-source signals to faults versus loads. Then after a dual-screening purification of statistical features, the BCS is deployed as a dual-purpose physical constraint linking the subsequent core modules. It first functions as a physical prior in a Physics-Embedded Channel Attention Mechanism to adaptively highlight fault signatures while suppressing load noise, and then acts as a regularization penalty within a Correlation-Regularized Stacked Autoencoder to constrain the deep fusion process. Driven by this sequential BCS guidance, the network ultimately condenses these refined representations into a highly robust, anti-load 1D Health Indicator. Validated through simulations and physical testbench experiments, the ACFN successfully disentangles complex coupled signals into a linearly separable manifold. It achieves a superior diagnostic accuracy of 95.24% under the 3 kN load. This physics-guided framework effectively bridges the gap between mechanistic interpretability and deep learning, providing a highly robust solution for EHA health management.

title: Physically driven multi-modal feature fusion for interpretable tool wear state identification in CFRP milling
