A single-loop reweighted numerical integration method for failure probability function estimation under parametric probability boxes
abstract: Estimating the failure probability function under parametric probability boxes (p-boxes), which capture mixed aleatory and epistemic uncertainties, remains computationally challenging, especially when expensive computer models are involved. To address this challenge, the present paper develops a single-loop reweighted numerical integration method for efficient estimation of the complete failure probability function and its bounds. The generalized failure probability function is reformulated through a reweighting scheme that employs an auxiliary density function. Since the theoretically optimal auxiliary function is intractable, we provide two practical and reliable alternatives. The suggested reweighted probability operation is then combined with Generalized F discrepancy-based point selection strategy to compute the reformulated failure probability in a single-loop manner. This point selection strategy partitions the uncertainty space into Voronoi cells and assigns a representative point with the associated probability to each cell, avoiding brute-force sampling. The framework is fully non-intrusive, as it relies solely on the input p-boxes without relying on the form of the performance function. Finally, four case studies: a mathematical example, a vehicle front axle, a 120-bar truss, and a nonlinear Duffing oscillator, demonstrate that the proposed method achieves high accuracy and efficiency, is applicable to nonlinear and dynamic problems, and integrates seamlessly with black-box simulation codes for complex engineering applications.

title: End-to-end virtual sensing with head tracking using a temporal convolutional network for active road noise control
A multi-scale frequency domain information-driven method for ultrasonic welding quality prediction
Modelling and characterization of the unzipping dynamics of dielectric fluid actuators
abstract: Dielectric Fluid Actuators (DFAs) are variable capacitors that contract as a result of electrostatic forces acting on a compliant multilayer structure composed of a polymer film and an insulating liquid. Differences in the dielectric time constants of the liquid and polymeric layers lead to charge retention at their interface, causing a decay in Maxwell stress that ultimately leads to a relaxation of the actuator stroke in the presence of a constant applied voltage. In this work, we introduce a new physics-based continuum framework that extends electrostatic force modelling from fixed parallel-plate capacitors to actuator-level modelling, by coupling continuum electrical dynamics with a lumped mechanical model of the DFA. The DFA is represented as a continuum of infinitesimal variable capacitors, each modelled using simple RC elements. The framework is experimentally validated on a simple multi-layer open-pouch DFA, and on an established layout of hydraulically amplified self-healing electrostatic actuator. Even with a simplified description of the material electrical response (e.g., constant resistivities) and lumped deformation mechanics, the framework captures the relevant trends in unzipping dynamics with respect to geometry and operating conditions (applied voltage and external forces). The proposed framework lays the foundations for electro-mechanical dynamic continuum modelling of DFAs.

title: Prior superpixel-driven multi-modal query hypergraph convolutional network for weld quality assessment
abstract: The quality of weld is critical to the reliability of structural connections and operational safety in applications such as automotive manufacturing, rail transportation, and aerospace. However, conventional single-modal welding quality assessment methods often suffer from limited information representation, weak robustness to interference, and poor adaptability to complex operating conditions. To address these limitations, this study proposes a prior superpixel-driven multi-modal query hypergraph convolutional network (PS-MQHGN) for high-precision weld quality evaluation. PS-MQHGN employs a cross-modal query hypergraph convolution module to explicitly model the information transfer pathways between different modalities, such as images and process signals, thereby achieving effective multimodal feature integration. In addition, a prior superpixel-driven dual-image interaction module is designed to actively focus on regions relevant to welding quality and to align up and down surface features based on label consistency. To further enhance performance, a dual-dimensional hypergraph feature aggregation mechanism is introduced to suppress the adverse influence of noise and weakly correlated hyperedges on model stability. In a representative resistance spot welding scenario, experimental results demonstrate that PS-MQHGN achieves high-precision weld quality prediction under complex welding conditions, with a mean absolute error of 0.1576 mm, corresponding to a 15.7% reduction compared with state-of-the-art models. PS-MQHGN provides reliable support for weld quality assessment and process control.

Internal combination resonance in a Micro Electro-Mechanical three-axis gyroscope: Experimental results and reduced-order modelling via invariant manifolds
abstract: This work investigates internal combination resonance in a Micro-Electro-Mechanical System (MEMS) three-axis gyroscope, where energy couples among three vibrational modes via the relationship ω1 + ω2 ≈ ω3 . The phenomenon is first characterised experimentally through frequency response measurements and spectrograms, revealing paired resonance peaks that emerge only under dual-frequency excitation. A theoretical framework grounded in complex normal form theory is then developed, deriving analytical expressions for the frequency-response curves which are shown to replicate the experimental findings. A reduced-order model of the fully coupled electromechanical problem is constructed via Direct Parametrisation of Invariant Manifolds applied to the full finite element mesh (1.3 million degrees of freedom), demonstrating quantitative agreement with experiments and validating the predicted mechanisms. By combining invariant manifold parametrisation with complex normal form theory, the methodology bridges the gap between analytical understanding and practical finite element reduction, yielding explicit solutions for nonlinear phenomena whilst maintaining computational efficiency for large-scale systems. The results validate invariant manifold methods as a robust tool for MEMS design and control applications.

Experimental investigation, mechanism analysis and mitigation solutions for tire hop during snap start of vehicles
abstract: During rapid vehicle startup on low-adhesion road surfaces, stick-slip friction between the tires and the pavement triggers self-excited vibration of the vehicle driveline system. This vibration induces drive shaft torque fluctuation, accompanied by powertrain and seat track vibration, a phenomenon formally defined as tire hop. Existing research lacks high-precision testing methods for transient drive shaft torque under tire hop. The influences of road conditions, driving modes and powertrain layouts on tire hop characteristics have not been systematically explored. Moreover, the formation mechanism of multi-frequency vibration peaks during tire hop remains unclear, and few studies consider the nonlinear features of powertrain mounts to analyze vibration characteristics or propose targeted suppression solutions. This paper presents several distinct innovations for tire hop research. Firstly, a wireless telemetry-based testing method is proposed to achieve high-precision measurement of transient drive shaft torque under tire hop conditions. Secondly, vehicle snap start experiments are conducted to systematically analyze how road surface states, different driving modes and diverse powertrain layout configurations affect key tire hop parameters. The parameters include oscillation of wheel speed and drive shaft torque, vibrations of powertrain vibration and seat track. Thirdly, a refined vibration model is established by taking the nonlinear force-displacement characteristics of powertrain mounts into account, which successfully uncovers the formation mechanism of multi-frequency vibration peaks. The relationship between powertrain output torque and inherent natural frequencies is also quantitatively investigated. Finally, a targeted optimization strategy is put forward by optimizing mount mechanical performance, quantity and arrangement to reduce tire hop-caused vibrations of powertrain mounts and seat tracks.

Early anomaly detection in wind Turbines by Causality-based graph attention networks
abstract: Early anomaly detection is a key issue for ensuring reliability, availability and efficiency in Wind Turbines (WTs) operation. Traditional condition monitoring techniques struggle to identify anomalies because of: i) the strong interconnections among the subsystems of a WT, which induce complex spatio-temporal dependencies in the measured signals and can enable the cascading propagation of the effects of anomalies, ii) the variability of the operating conditions, which can affect the anomaly signatures, and iii) the presence of control systems that can mask the anomalies signatures. To address these challenges, this work proposes a novel anomaly detection method employing a Graph Neural Network (GNN) autoencoder. GNN is selected for its capability in modeling the interconnected nature of subsystems and capturing the spatio-temporal dependencies in operational signals. A key contribution is the use of the Granger causality test to generate the GNN functional graph. By leveraging the causal relationships among turbine signals, the obtained graph ensures that the learned topology reflects the underlying physical dependencies rather than spurious correlations, as it may occur in traditional graphs. To handle variability of the operating conditions, graph attention layers adaptively weight sensor relationships, while gated recurrent units process the temporal dynamics. The proposed method is validated on synthetic data simulated using a high-fidelity WT model and applied to SCADA data collected from real WTs. Results demonstrate a 4% increase in recall and a 45% reduction in detection delay compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Strong–weak modal coupling in finite structures with antinode-concentrated resonators
abstract: Dynamic vibration absorbers (DVAs) and locally resonant metamaterials share a common physical foundation: subwavelength resonators coupled to a host structure. The two paradigms, however, have developed along parallel lines. DVA design on continuum hosts traditionally proceeds mode by mode, relying on modal truncation and iterative tuning. Metamaterial design rests on Bloch analysis of infinite periodic arrays, whose assumptions do not transfer to bounded structures with a finite number of resonators. As a result, neither paradigm captures the host–resonator interaction in such finite systems within a single governing relation. In this work, a unified closed-form framework is proposed for bounded continuum hosts equipped with a finite number of antinode-concentrated resonators. The host dynamic stiffness is expressed in a rational closed form, and the infinite modal sum is captured exactly. The optimal placement, tuning, and damping of all resonators follow simultaneously from a single characteristic equation, eliminating the iterative design process of conventional DVA theory. Within this single framework, a strong–weak mode coupling mechanism is identified. It reveals how a small number of finite resonators concentrated at antinodal positions can broaden the practical stopband well beyond the predictions of infinite-periodic metamaterial theory. The framework is validated against finite element analyses and beam experiments across a broadband range. The resulting closed-form expressions provide a practical, metamaterial-inspired design tool for broadband vibration suppression in finite continuum structures.

title: Calibration-light multi-point displacement measurement for railway bridge monitoring via a differential-form projection model
abstract: This study proposes a calibration-light framework for practical multi-point displacement monitoring of railway bridges using a single high-resolution video camera (and, when needed, two synchronized cameras for 3D reconstruction) with a wide-angle lens. The method enables synchronous displacement estimation during train passage without requiring full on-site calibration of external parameters. A differential-form projection model was developed to relate pixel movement to physical displacement increments in a bridge-fixed coordinate system, incorporating perspective-effect compensation via the pixel-to-displacement mapping (Eq. (15)), radial lens distortion correction, and camera-to-target distance estimation. Laboratory experiments demonstrated that the proposed method achieved accurate displacement estimation even under wide-angle imaging. Field applications to four railway bridges demonstrated the method’s practical applicability: Bridge A showed accurate vertical displacement consistent with velocimeter data; Bridge B revealed resonance and vibration modes across three spans; Bridge C demonstrated long-distance measurement (over 100 m) with span-specific modal characteristics; and Bridge D achieved 3D displacement estimation using two synchronized cameras consistent with laser Doppler velocimeter results at the same location. These results highlight the method’s practical applicability for bridge monitoring under diverse structural and environmental conditions.

title: Global optimization with structural reliability analysis methods
Physics-constrained neural parameter calibration of a Bouc-Wen hysteresis model for bolted joint assemblies
abstract: Bolted joints are characterized by friction-induced hysteresis and response dependence on excitation and tightening conditions, which complicates the calibration of reduced-order nonlinear models. A physics-constrained neural framework is introduced for calibrating a Bouc-Wen model using mean vibration records obtained under varying tightening torques. For each torque, a bounded neural generator proposes admissible model parameters, and a differentiable forward solver integrates displacement, velocity, and the model-internal hysteretic state. Calibration relies exclusively on measured velocity and measurement-derived displacement, while additional excitation levels are reserved for evaluating the torque-specific calibrated ensembles. Multiple independent calibration paths are maintained according to a prescribed convergence criterion and are organized using loss-informed empirical Gibbs weighting. Complete joint parameter vectors are then propagated to obtain time-domain, receptance, and hysteresis summaries. The results indicate torque-conditioned parameter organizations, consistent convergence behavior across most calibration paths, and close agreement with measured resonance locations. Propagation at excitation levels excluded from calibration further demonstrates that the calibrated ensembles can reproduce the principal amplitude-dependent response trends. The proposed framework thus offers a systematic approach for neural parameter calibration and empirical variability propagation, while preserving the prescribed Bouc-Wen dynamics throughout the inverse problem. • Physics-constrained neural calibration of Bouc-Wen bolted-joint parameters. • Mean-response calibrations are performed independently at two torques levels. • The unobserved hysteretic state is integrated using a measured-only loss. • Converged optimization paths form loss-informed joint empirical ensembles. • Frozen ensembles are propagated to amplitudes excluded from calibration.

title: TimeXer-based main bearing temperature prediction and Bayesian fault early warning for offshore wind turbines via transfer learning
Ultrasonic imaging modalities enabled by laser diffuse ultrasonic phased arrays
abstract: To perform a full matrix capture (FMC) with a laser-induced ultrasonic phased array, both the generation and detection lasers must be independently scanned to acquire signals from all combinations of source and receiver positions. In contrast, a laser diffuse ultrasonic phased array (LDUPA) enables rapid acquisition of an equivalent FMC dataset by scanning only a detection laser while ultrasound is generated from a fixed transducer. This FMC dataset is subsequently reconstructed by applying a diffuse correlation technique to the raw receive dataset. While the reconstructed FMC dataset is used for total focusing method (TFM) images, the early, coherent raw receive dataset can also be used directly to form images via a receive-only focusing method (RFM). This study compares ultrasound images generated from both the raw receive datasets and the reconstructed FMC datasets across various inspection configurations, including different transmitter positions and incident wave angles. Results from simulations and experiments show that the RFM images exhibit excellent detection capability within the incident wave’s illumination area, providing 2–5 dB higher signal to peak noise ratio compared to TFM images. In contrast, TFM images demonstrate good detection across the entire receiver aperture. The results also highlight the flexibility in transmitter positioning and incident wave angle, facilitating inspections that can adapt to accessibility constraints.

A general closed-form second-moment framework for probabilistic updating of damped MDOF systems
abstract: Probabilistic updating of damped structural systems lacks closed-form expressions for operator statistics, leaving iterative numerical methods or implicit auxiliary variable formulations that obscure analytical uncertainty propagation. This work develops a closed-form second-moment framework for simultaneous updating of mass, damping, and stiffness matrices under combined eigenvalue, eigenvector, and modal damping uncertainty, a combination for which explicit operator statistics were previously unavailable. The formulation exploits a sequential property of weighted Frobenius norm minimisation subject to modal orthogonality constraints, whereby the three updates are obtained in three successive convex steps. Stiffness updating depends only on measured frequencies, damping updating depends only on measured modal damping, and mass updating is deduced from the measured modal mass matrix through Berman’s incomplete-mode correction. Gaussian moment closures give exact mean operators, and Fréchet derivative-based perturbation expansions give Kronecker-structured sensitivity matrices that map modal uncertainty to physical-space operator covariance without auxiliary variables or nonlinear solvers. The cross-covariances between the identified modal quantities are retained throughout. Numerical verification on a non-proportionally damped benchmark confirms close analytical-Monte Carlo agreement for mean and covariance predictions, with cross-correlation inclusion yielding order-of-magnitude improvement over independence assumptions. The methodology exchanges finite-element sparsity for analytical tractability, positioning it as a component of digital twin applications, in which the updated operators are interpreted as reduced models condensed onto the instrumented degrees of freedom and the measured modes are taken to span that reduced space. In that setting operator-level uncertainty quantification supports probabilistic forward prediction, data assimilation, and lifecycle prognostics that sampling-based alternatives render prohibitive. The scope of the paper is the operator statistics themselves, and their embedding in a particular assimilation architecture is left open. The framework requires as many sensors as identified modes, with the analytical operators condensed onto those sensors, and it recovers the true mass exactly on the span of the identified modes.

Bayesian model updating via streamlined Bayesian active learning cubature
abstract: Bayesian model updating has been widely used for model calibration in engineering and scientific applications, as it not only updates model parameters but also quantifies their uncertainty. However, for computationally expensive models, efficiently estimating the model evidence (marginal likelihood) and the posterior distribution remains challenging. To address this issue, we propose a novel Bayesian active learning method for Bayesian model updating, which is termed as ‘Streamlined Bayesian Active Learning Cubature’ (SBALC). The core idea is to approximate the log-likelihood function using Gaussian process (GP) regression in a streamlined Bayesian active learning way. Rather than generating many samples from the posterior GP, we only use its mean and standard deviation function to form the model evidence estimator, stopping criterion, and learning function. Specifically, the estimation of model evidence is first treated as a Bayesian cubature problem, with a GP prior assigned over the log-likelihood function. Second, a plug-in estimator for model evidence is proposed based on the posterior mean function of the GP. Third, an upper bound on the expected absolute error between the posterior model evidence and its plug-in estimator is derived. Building on this result, a novel stopping criterion and learning function are proposed using only the posterior mean and standard deviation functions of the GP. Finally, we can obtain the model evidence based on the posterior mean function of the log-likelihood function in conjunction with Monte Carlo simulation, as well as the samples for the posterior distribution of model parameters as a by-product. Four numerical examples are presented to demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method compared to several existing approaches. The results show that the method can significantly reduce the number of model evaluations and the computational time without compromising accuracy.

title: Experimentally validated reduced-order modeling of gear-rotor-bearing systems with three-dimensional shaft compliance and gyroscopic mapping
Flexural-wave shielding in plates through scattering by a curved resonator arrangement
abstract: This study considers a thin elastic plate excited by a harmonic point force and coupled to locally resonant mass–spring attachments distributed along two opposing parabolic trajectories. The resulting resonator arrangement redirects part of the incident flexural-wave energy through repeated scattering along the curved interface, thereby reducing transmission beyond the curved array and producing a downstream shielded region. An analytical model is formulated within the Kirchhoff–Love plate framework, where the Green’s function of an unbounded plate is used to describe the dynamic interaction between the host structure and the resonators. Three-dimensional finite-element simulations are used to verify the analytical predictions and characterize the redistribution of the wave field around the resonator arrangement. Experimental measurements are performed on an aluminum plate equipped with a water-jet-cut resonator arrangement using scanning laser Doppler vibrometry. The combined analytical, numerical, and experimental results show that the curved resonator arrangement produces a pronounced vibration-shielding zone beyond the resonator interface, with a substantial reduction in transmitted flexural-wave amplitude. Parametric analyses quantify the effects of curvature, normalized resonator spacing, and excitation frequency. The resulting design maps identify spacing regimes that minimize the shielded response and provide practical guidelines for curvature-based wave-shielding designs in continuous plate structures.

title: Adaptive event-triggered soft actor-critic control for MR suspension subject to actuator smoothness constraints
An integrated autoencoder-based framework for unsupervised domain adaptation in structural health monitoring of bridges
abstract: The limited availability of long-term bridge-monitoring data presents a significant obstacle to the application of machine learning in structural health monitoring (SHM). Domain adaptation offers a means of addressing this data scarcity, but existing methods often have limited generalization and are sensitive to hyperparameter choices. This study proposes a reconstruction-based domain adaptation framework in which target-domain observations are geometrically aligned with the latent space learned by an autoencoder trained on data from a source bridge and, subsequently, reconstructed using its decoder. Unlike conventional feature-alignment approaches, the proposed formulation transfers the reconstruction model itself, enabling target-domain evaluation without labels, classifier retraining, or threshold recalibration. The autoencoder is trained on baseline data collected during commissioning of the source bridge, using observations composed of natural frequencies as damage-sensitive features. Adaptation is performed through orthogonal Procrustes alignment in the latent space, followed by reconstruction with the source-trained decoder. Validation using the Z24 Bridge dataset demonstrates that the framework mitigates seasonal domain shift while preserving sensitivity to controlled damage. The approach is then transferred to a twin bridge over the Itacaiúnas River using only latent-space alignment and no model retraining. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework enables damage assessment across bridges while substantially reducing the data and training requirements for practical deployment.

Deep reinforcement learning for semi-active structural control using a variable inerter device
abstract: Structural control devices employing inerters have attracted considerable attention owing to their superior vibration mitigation performance. Variable inerter devices, which enable real-time adjustment of inertance and damping, offer further performance enhancement but also introduce a challenging nonlinear control problem. This paper proposes a deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based control strategy for a tuned variable inertial mass electromagnetic transducer (TVIMET) installed in a five-story base-isolated building. The proposed controller is developed using recurrent proximal policy optimization (RPPO) with long short-term memory (LSTM) networks to account for both the partially observable nature of practical structural control and the history-dependent nonlinear behavior of the lead–rubber bearing (LRB) isolation system. Numerical simulations are conducted under a wide range of earthquake excitations, and the proposed method is compared with passive base isolation, a passive tuned viscous mass damper (TVMD), and a semi-active tuned inertial mass electromagnetic transducer (TIMET). The proposed TVIMET successfully adapts both the inertance and damping coefficient according to the changing dynamic characteristics of the structure. Unlike the passive TVMD, which is designed assuming post-yield structural behavior, the proposed controller remains effective even under earthquake excitations that do not induce significant yielding of the isolation layer. It also achieves the best overall vibration reduction, particularly in terms of the RMS structural responses. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of simultaneously adapting the inertance and damping through DRL for nonlinear structural vibration control.

Performance-based probabilistic RUL prediction via particle filtering with neural-guided inference
abstract: Accurate prediction of the Remaining Useful Life (RUL) is essential for efficient operations and predictive maintenance of industrial systems. Prognostics is traditionally structured as a two-step procedure comprising estimation of the current system condition and prediction of future behavior and condition. Many data-driven approaches map sensor measurements directly to RUL without explicitly modeling degradation dynamics. We propose a data-driven prognostic framework that preserves this estimation–prediction structure without requiring physics-based state models. In the estimation stage, health indices are inferred from sensor measurements. Degradation parameters are treated probabilistically and inferred within a Bayesian framework, with online sequential updates via particle filtering. In the prediction stage, the stochastic degradation model is evaluated conditioned on the inferred parameter posterior, yielding an RUL distribution as a random variable with a hitting time. An offline-trained neural network serves as a particle-filter (PF) controller to improve adaptability while maintaining principled uncertainty propagation. Evaluation on the N-CMAPSS benchmark demonstrates competitive RUL accuracy and statistically grounded uncertainty across operating conditions, and comparisons indicate the advantages of explicitly separating estimation from prediction in data-driven prognostics.

title: Calculation method and topology optimization design of phononic crystal considering discrepancies from ideal 2D models
Tool-grounded large language models for decision-level fusion in fault diagnosis
abstract: Modern condition-monitoring systems generate heterogeneous information, such as high-rate sensor streams, derived health indicators, and discrete event histories, that must be combined into actionable diagnostic statements. Large language models (LLMs) are attractive as a decision-level fusion mechanism because they natively handle the textual modality, but their use in safety-critical fault diagnosis is impeded by hallucinated numerical content and stochastic outputs. This paper proposes a two-level information-fusion framework that uses an LLM as a constrained fusion operator rather than as a generator of facts. At the feature level, a recursive joint state-and-fault estimator built on a linear state-space model produces a vector of derived indicators, including an estimate of the actuator-fault parameter and its uncertainty. At the decision level, the LLM is restricted to interact with the estimator state and the event history exclusively through a finite library of typed deterministic tools, and must copy every numerical token in its response from a tool output. Grounding of the response is then satisfied by construction, and consistency follows once the sequence of tool calls is fixed. The framework is illustrated on a realistic actuator-fault scenario in which an autopilot-driven autonomous surface vessel encounters three fault events of different characters and the LLM produces reproducible operator-facing reports. A structured comparison against the two alternative reporting architectures available for this task, a rule-based template reporter driven by the same estimator and a flat-prompt LLM given the same numerical context, identifies open-ended query coverage at fixed numerical reliability as the property that neither alternative provides, and states the metrics under which that claim is to be tested.

Honeycomb metamaterial panel with core grid of wire-masses resonators for tuneable vibration and sound radiation bandgap
abstract: Controlling flexural vibrations and sound radiation in thin-walled structures subjected to time-varying tonal excitations remains a major engineering challenge. While acoustic metamaterials have demonstrated significant potential for vibration attenuation, most tuneable designs rely on complex architectures that hinder practical implementation. This study proposes a lightweight composite panel integrating a simple honeycomb-core elastic metamaterial capable of generating a continuously tuneable flexural vibration bandgap. The proposed concept consists of a tensioned wire routed in a continuous zigzag path through the honeycomb cells, with concentrated masses attached at the centre of each cell. Each wire–mass subsystem acts as a base-excited resonator whose natural frequency is controlled by the wire tension. The resulting periodic array of identical resonators enables continuous tuning of the resonance frequency and the associated flexural vibration stopband without modifying the structural layout. The design methodology is presented and validated through simulations and experimental testing of a prototype panel. The results demonstrate the formation of both flexural vibration and sound radiation stopband with maximum attenuations of 25 dB and 20 dB respectively. By varying the wire tension, the stopband can be shifted over a frequency range of approximately 300 Hz, allowing adaptive suppression of time-varying tonal disturbances. The proposed metamaterial combines structural simplicity, low mass, ease of implementation, and robust, broadband-tuneable dynamic behaviour, providing an effective strategy for adaptive vibration and noise control in lightweight engineering structures operating under variable excitation conditions, including aerospace, automotive, marine, and industrial applications.

Hybrid testing of wind turbine components using Kane’s method
abstract: Hybrid testing combines numerical simulations with physical experiments to evaluate large mechanical systems, such as wind turbines, that are impractical to test at full scale. While hybrid testing has been widely applied in structural dynamics, its extension to complex multibody dynamic systems remains challenging due to nonlinear kinematics and strongly coupled degrees of freedom. Although Kane’s method underpins widely used wind turbine simulation tools, hybrid testing frameworks that directly integrate Kane-based multibody formulations and interface force coupling remain largely unexplored. Here, a stepwise hybrid testing framework is presented in which the equations of motion are formulated using Kane’s method, enabling a systematic treatment of multibody dynamics within hybrid testing. Interface forces are identified from free-body diagrams and incorporated into the equations of motion through the principle of virtual power, allowing consistent coupling between numerical and physical substructures. The framework is demonstrated in a pseudo-dynamic hybrid test of a 13-degree-of-freedom simplified wind turbine rotor system, where a pitch bearing is tested as a physical substructure under force-controlled bi-axial bending and displacement-controlled pitch rotation. A virtual hybrid test validates the formulation and coordination algorithm, while the physical hybrid test demonstrates stable mixed-mode coupling under experimental feedback. The results show that the framework can couple a Kane-based multibody model with a physical wind turbine component and capture its influence on the system-level rotor response.

title: Control-Based Continuation for self-oscillating systems: Application to flow induced vibrations
abstract: An enhanced version of Control-Based Continuation (CBC) is proposed to carry out experimental continuation on self-sustained systems, whose working frequency is not known a priori . Our approach combines three main stages: an online frequency tracking algorithm using an embedded phase-locked loop, an online noninvasive CBC stabilization loop using adaptive filters, and a derivative free arc continuation algorithm. As a proof of concept, it is implemented to study an elementary aero-vibro-acoustical model of buzzing lips that exhibits self-sustained oscillations with a wide range of fundamental frequency. The model relies on interactions between an acoustical resonator (the air column) and an oscillating valve (the lips) through a nonlinear flow. The Control-Based Continuation is implemented without taking advantage of the modeling equations, mimicking a real experiment. This results in a pseudo-experimental bifurcation diagram, showing strong accordance with virtual open-loop testing and numerical continuation, which proves robustness of our method.
